slides.text: For thirty years, police detectives have brought me the wristwatches of the dead. A mechanical movement is an incorruptible witness: when a body hits the river or a bullet shatters a crystal, the balance wheel freezes at the exact second of impact. Yesterday, Inspector Morel placed a gold Patek Philippe on my workbench—pulled from the wrist of a shipping magnate whose yacht sank at 2:15 AM.

The hands read 2:17 AM, matching the coast guard distress call. Morel just needed my signature to close the accidental drowning file. But when I screwed my jeweler's loupe into my eye and unscrewed the sapphire caseback, my tweezers froze. The interior gears were bone-dry. Not a single drop of saltwater had breached the gasket. Someone had opened the casing and jammed a human eyelash into the escapement wheel.

More unsettling still was the perpetual calendar disc beneath the dial. The killer had manually wound the date forward by twenty-four hours—to tomorrow's date—and scratched a six-digit locker number into the gold rotor weight. Before I could call Morel back into the shop, the tiny alarm complication inside the dead man's watch clicked, whirred, and began to chime.
